public_rationale: On June 6, 2025, TechCrunch reported unnamed sources saying Cursor had surpassed $500 million in annual recurring revenue, without specifying the calculation needed to reconcile it with the claimed annualized revenue [e1]. On July 4, Cursor said most users’ costs had stayed fairly constant, while the hardest requests cost an order of magnitude more than simple ones [e2]. Cursor’s explanation of its pricing change provides no matched revenue and serving-cost figures showing whether the former offering was economically unsustainable [e2]. These items settle neither affordability under the former terms nor the suggested financial weakness across coding startups [e1, e2].
limitations: The reported ARR figure is not reconciled to the claimed annualized-revenue measure.
The packet lacks matched revenue, realized serving costs, customer usage distribution and margins under the former terms.
Differences in request costs and a pricing change establish neither sustainability nor unsustainability of the former offering.
The evidence does not test the broader inference about coding startups.

public_payload.normalized_proposition: Cursor reached $500 million in annualized revenue selling a product it can no longer afford to sell, which points to material weakness at Cursor and at all coding startups.

statement.excerpt: To put it bluntly: Cursor's growth story was a lie. It reached $500 million in annualized revenue selling a product it can no longer afford to sell, suggesting material weakness in its own business and any and all coding startups.
statement.document_title: The Hater's Guide To The AI Bubble

from_speaker: Cursor's growth story was a lie
a product it can no longer afford to sell
our_interpretation: The context identifies a June 2025 revenue milestone and changes to the offering before publication on July 21.
Cannot afford means the former offering was economically unsustainable at its existing price and usage terms, rather than that Cursor was insolvent.
Growth story was a lie is read as criticism of the offering's sustainability, not as a separately evidenced allegation that the revenue figure was fabricated.
The industry-wide conclusion is introduced as a suggestion; it is not treated as an independently quantified claim about every startup.
The run-rate figure is treated as a press-reported estimate. ARR terminology must not silently substitute for a disclosed monthly-revenue calculation.
criteria.support_condition: Evidence establishes the stated annualized revenue milestone and shows that the former offering's actual serving costs made its continued sale economically unsustainable.
criteria.contradiction_condition: Matching records disprove the revenue milestone or show that the former offering could sustainably cover its relevant costs. Funding or subsequent growth alone does not establish affordability.

evidence.explanation: Cursor explains the move to usage-based terms through differences in request costs. It supplies neither aggregate margins nor evidence that the entire former offering was unaffordable; its statement about most users also limits that inference.

public_payload.what_would_resolve: Records covering June 1–July 21, 2025 that reconcile the revenue measure and match revenue under the former terms with realized serving costs and customer usage, sufficient to determine whether continued sales could sustainably cover relevant costs. Comparable financial evidence from other coding startups would be needed to assess the broader industry inference.
